title: How Should a Pastor Prepare a Couple for Marriage?
subtitle: On premarital work, the ceremony, and refusing to let the wedding eclipse the marriage you are preparing

sections.title: The Day and the Decades
sections.body:
A couple comes to you glowing, and they want to talk about the day. The venue, the colors, the order of the processional, whether you will wear the robe. They have spent a year and a fortune on a single afternoon.

You are not there to officiate an afternoon. You are there to prepare a marriage that has to survive forty years of Tuesdays.

The wedding industry has done something quiet and ruinous. It has taught two people to pour every ounce of attention into the most photographed and least important day of their union, and then to wake up the next morning married and unprepared. I have watched couples plan a flawless ceremony and a doomed marriage and never notice the difference, because no one made them look at the second thing. That is partly the pastor's fault. We get swept into the romance and forget that the romance is not the point. The vow is the point. The vow is a promise to a person you have not met yet, the person your spouse will become, and your job is to make sure they understand what they are about to swear before God.

sections.title: The Work Before the Wedding
sections.body:
Do not marry strangers. Make the premarital sessions a condition, not a suggestion, and tell them so the first time they ask, because the couple that resents the preparation is often the couple that needs it most.

Meet several times. Real sessions, not one hurried coffee. There is no shortcut here that does not cost someone later.

Get underneath the glow to the things that actually break marriages. How do they handle money, and have they ever once looked at each other's debt and spending and assumptions about it. How do they handle conflict, because everyone is gracious while in love and the real question is who they become when they are angry and tired. What did marriage look like in the houses they grew up in, because each of them is carrying a blueprint they have never examined and they will build from it without knowing. Talk about sex honestly. Talk about children, about in-laws, about faith, about the day one of them stops feeling in love and has to decide whether the vow still holds when the feeling does not. Use a tool if it helps you, an inventory that surfaces what they will not raise on their own. And watch for the things that should slow a wedding down. Watch for control dressed as care, for contempt, for a pattern of fear in one of them around the other. If you see those, you have a harder job than officiating. You have the job of love that is willing to say not yet, and a pastor who will not risk an awkward conversation to prevent a ruinous marriage is not loving the couple. He is loving his own comfort.

sections.title: The Ceremony Itself
sections.body:
Now the day comes, and you stand between them, and a few hundred people are watching. Many of them have troubled marriages of their own, and some are divorced, and the ceremony is preaching to all of them whether you intend it or not.

So make the ceremony mean something. A wedding is a worship service, not a stage production, and you are the one responsible for keeping that true.

Keep your part short and weighty. Do not perform. The couple is nervous, the crowd is warm, and a long homily will be remembered as the part that ran too long. Say a few true things about what marriage is, that it is a covenant and not a contract, that it images something about Christ and the church that is larger than the two people standing there, that the vows they are about to make are made before God who hears them and will hold them to them. Let the vows be real vows, the old hard words about sickness and poverty and worse, because those words are doing a job. They are telling two people in love that love alone will not be enough, and that they are promising to stay when love runs thin. Pronounce the blessing like you mean it. Then get out of the way. The day belongs to them and to God. You are the witness, not the show.

sections.title: When You Should Hesitate
sections.body:
Not every couple should be married, and not every couple should be married by you, and the pressure to say yes is enormous because the date is set and the deposits are paid and a refusal will cost you.

Say it anyway when you must. A wedding you should not perform is not a favor to anyone in it.

There is the couple already living as married, sleeping together for years, who want the church's stamp on something they never treated as holy. You can marry them, but do not pretend the preparation is unnecessary, and do not let the ceremony bless a casualness God does not bless. There is the couple where one believes and one does not, and you owe them an honest conversation about what they are building on a foundation they do not share. There is the couple racing to the altar to outrun a fear, or a pregnancy, or a parent, and speed is rarely the friend of a good decision. And there is the couple where something in you, watching them, goes quiet and uneasy. Trust that. You have sat with more marriages than they have, and you can sometimes see the cliff they cannot. Your job is not to forbid. Your job is to tell the truth in love and let them decide in front of it. I have married couples I should have made wait. I felt the unease and I overrode it because saying so was hard. Some of those marriages are gone now. The hard conversation is cheaper than the divorce.

sections.title: Marrying Them Into a People
sections.body:
The honeymoon ends, the gifts are put away, and a new marriage steps into the ordinary, and the ordinary is where marriages are won and lost. A wedding takes a day. A marriage takes a community.

Do not marry a couple and release them. Marry them into a people.

The modern marriage is asked to carry a weight it was never meant to carry alone, two people expected to be each other's entire world with no one around them. That is a crushing load, and it crushes. So weave the couple into the body. Connect them to older couples who have already walked the road and survived its potholes, who can tell a young husband that the year he is dreading is survivable because they survived it. Check on them at the one year mark, the place where the romance has cooled and the work has not yet been learned. Tell them on the wedding day that you are not finished with them, that the church that witnessed their vows intends to help them keep them. A marriage held by a community is a marriage with a fighting chance. You did not just perform a ceremony. You added a covenant to a congregation, and now you help them keep it. That is the work. The afternoon was never the point.
